dailyBrief.text: Good morning, Smileys — Benji is five days old, and it's a cold, damp Friday to stay in with him. Overnight, Iran sent a nuclear proposal to the U.S. through Qatar tied to seven demands, while tankers keep getting hit in the Strait of Hormuz, and chip stocks are bouncing this morning after Thursday's 5.52% Nasdaq drop into correction. Solon tops out near 49° with temperatures falling through the day and showers likely by evening, so any errands are better done early. Tonight is a sports doubleheader from the couch: Ohio State hoops opens at home against Youngstown State at 6:30 PM, and the Cavs host the 8-1 76ers at 7:30 PM in an NBA Cup game, with Jarrett Allen questionable. Locally, the Ohio Hazmat Teams Conference runs today and tomorrow at the Solon Community Center.

weekBrief.text: Benji's first week wraps up as a quiet, stay-home stretch — born Sunday, home Tuesday, pediatrician Wednesday, and now five days old with the house settling into a rhythm around him. Solon's weather turns cold and damp for the weekend — 49° with evening showers Friday and 46° Saturday — then breaks sunny and warmer Sunday at 57°, peaking near 61° Tuesday before cooling again. The sports weekend is stacked: the Cavs host Philadelphia tonight and the Knicks Saturday, Ohio State football hosts Oregon Saturday afternoon, and the Browns visit the Saints Sunday with Shedeur Sanders in line for his first start of the season. The week's standout grocery move stays the Thanksgiving stock-up — Meijer brand frozen turkeys at 79¢/lb or less through November 26 beat Giant Eagle's 95¢/lb — and if energy allows, Hadestown continues at Playhouse Square this weekend.

Iran sends a nuclear proposal to the U.S. through Qatar — with seven demands first
items.summary:
Iran has passed a nuclear proposal to Washington through Qatari mediators, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Thursday. Tehran says the proposal will only be discussed once the United States meets seven demands it has set out first.

Qatari officials have been meeting Iranian counterparts since last week, and the issues on the table go well beyond the nuclear file itself. They include the future of the Strait of Hormuz, the American blockade on Iranian ports, sanctions relief, and whether formal nuclear talks can restart at all.

Both sides acknowledge they remain far apart, which makes this an opening move rather than a breakthrough. What to watch is whether Washington answers the demands publicly, and whether the channel through Qatar produces an actual negotiating date.

items.title: Tankers keep getting hit in the Strait of Hormuz after the U.S. election
items.summary:
Iran reported three more tankers damaged in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday — two that struck naval mines and a third that caught fire, according to the Revolutionary Guards. The British maritime agency UKMTO counts at least five vessel incidents since Sunday alone.

October was the worst month yet, with 35 vessels hit. Oil markets have been whipsawing through it: prices dropped sharply in recent days as traders bet a chastened Washington might hold off on new strikes, then edged back up on Thursday.

Vice President JD Vance has publicly blamed the war for Republicans' midterm losses, while two sources told Reuters the president may still order a return to hostilities now that voting is over. For drivers and shippers alike, the strait remains the single biggest wild card in energy prices.

items.title: Israel's president will wait until Sunday to pick who tries to form a government
items.summary:
Israeli President Isaac Herzog wrapped up two days of consultations with every party in the Knesset on Thursday and said he will not announce until Sunday who gets the first chance to form a government. Lawmakers backing Gadi Eisenkot totaled 67 recommendations, against 46 for incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

The arithmetic is the problem. Final results from the October 27 election gave Netanyahu's bloc 53 seats, Eisenkot's bloc 48, and Arab-led parties a record 19 — nobody holds the 61 needed for a majority in the 120-seat parliament. Herzog pointed to mutual vetoes between and within the blocs and said he will hold personal talks with party leaders first.

Whoever is picked gets 28 days, with a possible two-week extension, and Netanyahu stays on as caretaker prime minister in the meantime. The new Knesset is expected to be sworn in November 10, so Sunday's choice sets the clock for weeks of coalition bargaining.

items.title: Russia and Ukraine trade overnight strikes while rebuilding talks go on in Brussels
items.summary:
Russia and Ukraine exchanged another heavy round of airstrikes overnight into Thursday, even as officials gathered at NATO headquarters in Brussels for a second day of talks on reconstruction and security. Ukraine said its defenses downed or suppressed 105 of 128 Russian attack drones, with strikes wounding four people in the Dnipropetrovsk and Kyiv regions.

Russia said it intercepted 496 Ukrainian drones across 13 regions and Crimea, and officials in occupied Luhansk reported five people killed there. In Brussels, lead Ukrainian negotiator Rustem Umerov said the agenda covered postwar rebuilding, funding for 2027, and security guarantees, with the U.S., Britain, France, Germany, the EU, NATO, the World Bank and BlackRock all represented.

The meetings are a runway to next week's planned talks in Abu Dhabi, where Russian, Ukrainian and American negotiators are due to try to end the war. Fighting at this intensity, days before a peace table convenes, is each side negotiating with leverage as much as with words.

items.title: Pope Leo starts his longest trip yet — Uruguay, Argentina and Peru — weeks after surgery
items.summary:
Pope Leo XIV left Rome on Friday to begin a 12-day, three-country tour of Latin America, the longest and farthest trip of his pontificate. He is due in Montevideo, Uruguay, after a 13-and-a-half-hour flight, just three weeks after lung cancer surgery on October 13.

The itinerary is demanding: a visit to a Montevideo neighborhood struggling with gang violence, Masses in Paysandú and Florida, then Argentina — the first papal visit there in 39 years, including a meeting with President Javier Milei — and finally Peru. Peru is personal territory: Leo served there as a missionary priest and as bishop of Chiclayo for two decades, and he holds Peruvian citizenship.

Latin America is home to roughly 40 percent of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics, but the Catholic share of the population has been shrinking, and Uruguay is the region's most secular country. The trip is both a homecoming and a test of the church's hold in a region where it is losing ground.

items.title: Paraguay's president resigns and is impeached after a digital bank collapse
items.summary:
Paraguay's President Santiago Peña announced his resignation on Thursday, and within minutes the lower house of Congress voted 78-0 to impeach him anyway. The attorney general has opened three criminal investigations tied to the collapse of Ueno Bank, which the central bank seized on Tuesday.

Ueno's capital ratio had fallen to less than half the legal minimum, and customer deposits, apps and cards were frozen. The bank held about $800 million in public money — including pension and health funds — and served roughly 3 million customers, about 60 percent of Paraguay's adults. A judge has jailed six bank executives, including its founder and president, pending trial.

Congress was still voting Friday on whether to accept the resignation, which would let Vice President Pedro Alliana take over without a Senate trial. Opposition senators want formal removal instead, arguing a quiet resignation would preserve Peña's lifetime Senate seat and legal protections. Peña, a former shareholder in the firm that owned the bank until last year, denies wrongdoing.

items.title: Democrats win both the House and the Senate in a midterm rout
items.summary:
Democrats have captured majorities in both chambers of Congress after Tuesday's vote, flipping Republican Senate seats in states including Texas, Kansas, Iowa, Ohio, North Carolina and South Carolina. One AP-based tally puts Democrats at at least 54 Senate seats, with the House count still provisional as late races are called.

Turnout was enormous for a midterm: more than 122 million people voted, close to 49 percent of eligible voters and near the 2018 high-water mark. Races in Mississippi and Alaska remained too close to call, with Democratic challengers leading in both.

The new majorities are promising affordability legislation, an end to the Iran war, reversals of Medicaid and SNAP cuts, AI and data-center rules, and investigations backed by subpoena power. The president is signaling vetoes in return, so January's handover sets up two years of open conflict between Congress and the White House.

items.title: Elizabeth Warren is about to run the Senate Banking Committee, and Wall Street is bracing
items.summary:
Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts is set to take over the Senate Banking Committee in January, with subpoena power over the country's biggest financial firms. Banks, private equity, crypto companies and prediction markets are all expecting a far more aggressive oversight era.

Her likely agenda includes a long-standing bill to rein in private-equity deals, probes into alleged insider trading on prediction markets, consumer protections in crypto, and questions about bankers' ties to Jeffrey Epstein. Allies such as Richard Blumenthal on investigations and Maxine Waters, the front-runner for House Financial Services, would extend that reach.

Markets noticed immediately: the S&P 500 fell more than 4 percent Thursday, with JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs each down over 4 percent, as investors priced in a tougher climate for finance and the AI boom. Warren wrote Thursday that Democrats won by promising to side with working people — and that working people expect delivery.

items.title: The 2028 Republican race is already on as leaders blame the Iran war and tariffs
items.summary:
Barely three days after the midterms, the Republican autopsy has turned into an opening round of the 2028 presidential race. Vice President JD Vance blamed the losses above all on the Iran war, writing that everyone knows why the party lost. Senator Ted Cruz called the result a blue tsunami and a historic repudiation, pointing at tariffs for making everything more expensive.

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis described the night as close to an extinction-level event for Republicans in much of the country, while noting Florida held. Democrats' 13-point win in the national popular vote was the biggest midterm margin since 1976, and Texas — where Republicans lost every statewide race — suddenly looks like a top 2028 battleground with 40 electoral votes.

Vance and Cruz are both widely expected to run, DeSantis is a possible candidate, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio is in the conversation but has stayed quiet. The president, asked about Vance, said only that maybe he runs and maybe he doesn't — an unusually lukewarm blessing this early.

items.title: Defense Secretary Hegseth is on thin ice, with an impeachment push possible next week
items.summary:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is the most exposed member of the Cabinet after Tuesday's losses, according to Axios reporting. One Trump adviser put it bluntly: Hegseth is definitely on thin ice, though that does not automatically mean the president forces him out.

The pressure is coming from two directions at once. The Iran war he championed — with the rosiest predictions of how quickly it would end — is deeply unpopular, and the House could vote as early as next week on an impeachment measure, sponsored by Republican Thomas Massie, accusing him of defying Congress and illegally continuing the war.

Publicly, the president stood by Hegseth on Wednesday, saying he is doing a very good job. Privately, an administration official predicted accountability would come during the lame-duck period before the new Congress takes over on January 3. Watch whether the impeachment vote is actually scheduled — that is the tell.

items.title: Vance privately blasts Netanyahu as the Iran war splits the administration
items.summary:
Vice President JD Vance has privately accused Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of being wrong on everything about the Iran war, according to reporting cited by Fox News. Vance leads a faction of senior officials urging the president to negotiate an end to the conflict, and he said publicly this week that the war is why Republicans lost.

Netanyahu had pushed Washington to resume strikes on Iran before the midterms; the president held off. Polling referenced in the reporting shows roughly six in ten voters opposed the war, which is why the argument inside the administration is as much political as military.

On Thursday the president held his first post-election national security meeting and said a decision on Iran is coming soon — with new strikes, continued economic pressure, and a negotiated deal all still on the table. A carrier group is not expected in the region before mid-November, which bounds how fast any military option could move.

items.title: Nasdaq futures climb as chip stocks stabilize after the steep AI selloff
items.summary:
Chip stocks bounced in early Friday trading after Thursday's rout, the Nasdaq's deepest one-day drop in 19 months, which confirmed a correction. By 4:14 a.m. Eastern, Nasdaq 100 futures were up about 1.5 percent, Nvidia had recovered 3.6 percent, and AMD, Intel, Broadcom and Micron were up between 5 and 8 percent.

Thursday's selling followed the Democratic midterm sweep, including wins in key data-center states, and fed fears that Congress could slow the AI buildout. One Jefferies strategist called the selloff reactionary rather than a fundamental reset — a collision of worries about AI spending, policy and inflation rather than broken businesses.

The next test arrives quickly: the October jobs report at 8:30 a.m. Friday, with traders pricing better than a 65 percent chance of a December rate hike. A fragile rebound plus a hot jobs number is exactly the combination that could restart the slide.

items.title: Tech selloff wipes out hedge fund gains, prompting risk cuts and layoffs
items.summary:
The global tech selloff has erased this year's gains at many hedge funds, and some managers are responding by cutting risk and shrinking their investment teams. Equity long-short funds focused on tech fell more than 4 percent on Thursday alone, leaving them roughly flat for the year, according to Goldman Sachs estimates.

That is a long fall from a peak gain of 24 percent in June, before the AI trade began unwinding. The $17 billion fund Walleye Capital told investors Thursday it will trim its internal equity long-short business and reduce a substantial part of its equity team, after its worst month since March 2020.

October set the tone: the Nasdaq 100 fell 6.6 percent, its worst month in a year and a half, as expensive AI borrowing and doubts about returns chipped at sentiment. When crowded trades unwind, the selling feeds itself — which is why fund managers are cutting exposure before they are forced to.

items.title: AI backlash could threaten Anthropic's IPO timing, potential investors say
items.summary:
Investors lined up for Anthropic's blockbuster stock offering are questioning whether the AI company can still start its roadshow next week and list in November as planned. The sharpest tech selloff in a year, plus post-election uncertainty, has clouded the calendar for new offerings generally.

Price is the other sticking point. A valuation around $1.5 trillion has been discussed, and some investors see that as the top of the range — they are pushing for a bigger discount, knowing the company needs the cash given its quarterly losses and huge commitments to AI infrastructure partners. Anthropic declined to comment.

The stakes reach beyond one company. Anthropic's debut was meant to be the proof that giant AI listings can still command giant prices; a delay or a cut-price deal would tell every other AI firm waiting in line to lower its expectations.

items.title: Wall Street's week ahead: inflation data is the next test after the tech swoon
items.summary:
Investors head into next week with the market on shaky footing. The Nasdaq closed Thursday nearly 12 percent below its October 6 record high, the S&P 500's tech sector sank 7.3 percent in a day, and the Philadelphia chip index tumbled more than 12 percent — the worst one-day drops for both in over six years.

The calendar offers little rest. Tuesday brings the October Consumer Price Index, the inflation reading that will shape the Federal Reserve's December meeting, and earnings arrive from CoreWeave, Applied Materials and Cisco — three very different windows into whether AI spending is holding up.

Futures still suggest roughly a 65 percent chance the Fed raises rates on December 8-9, with about two quarter-point hikes expected in this cycle. For context, the major indexes are still up for the year, with the S&P 500 ahead more than 7 percent — this is a correction inside a bull market, so far, not yet something worse.

items.title: Krispy Kreme was a sweet spot in Thursday's sour market
items.summary:
While investors fled chip and AI stocks on Thursday, Krispy Kreme quietly had its best day in ages, closing about 30 percent higher. The doughnut chain beat expectations on both the top and bottom lines, with third-quarter revenue of $328.8 million against estimates near $316 million.

Adjusted earnings came in at six cents a share versus the one cent analysts expected, and the company raised its full-year revenue guidance to between $1.35 and $1.40 billion. It has also slashed capital spending by roughly 65 percent from a year earlier as it works through a turnaround plan.

The fine print matters: Krispy Kreme still posted a net loss of $13.3 million for the quarter, and revenue actually fell 12.4 percent from a year ago after a rough stretch that included a breakup with McDonald's. Thursday's jump says investors liked the discipline — not that the turnaround is finished.

items.title: India's Coforge joins SpaceX's partner network to deploy Grok AI tools
items.summary:
Indian IT services firm Coforge said Friday it has joined the SpaceX Super Intelligence Partner Network, a program for helping companies build the Grok AI portfolio into their day-to-day operations. Coforge will act as a transformation partner, developing industry-specific Grok solutions inside clients' existing systems.

The work will run through Momentuum Blue, Coforge's engineering unit, which embeds teams of engineers and AI agents inside client organizations and ties projects to agreed business targets. Financial terms of the partnership were not disclosed.

It is a small deal with a telling shape: while public markets punish AI spending, enterprise firms are still signing up to deploy the technology. Grok's toolkit spans chat, research, analysis, software development and image and video generation — the unglamorous integration work is where the steady money is.

items.title: Wisconsin infant dies of measles — the state's first measles death since 1990
items.summary:
Wisconsin health officials announced Thursday that an infant in the southwestern part of the state has died in connection with the ongoing measles outbreak, with the coroner listing measles as the immediate cause. It is Wisconsin's first measles death in 36 years, and officials declined to release further details to protect the family's privacy.

The state had reported 431 cases across 13 counties as of November 3, with nine people hospitalized — its largest caseload in more than 35 years. All but three cases were in unvaccinated people, according to the Associated Press.

Nationally, the CDC has counted more than 4,800 confirmed measles cases this year across 45 states and Washington, D.C. — more than double last year's total — as outbreaks grow in communities where childhood vaccination rates have slipped. Health officials continue to point to vaccination as the clearest line of protection, especially for infants too young to be fully immunized.

items.title: 'Catastrophic' flooding forces more than 100 rescues on the Georgia–Tennessee border
items.summary:
Historic flooding overwhelmed the twin towns of McCaysville, Georgia, and Copperhill, Tennessee, on Thursday, forcing more than 100 rescues as their shared river climbed to a record crest of 18.05 feet — above the previous record set in 1990. Flash flood emergencies, the highest level of flood warning, were issued for both towns.

Between three and six inches of rain fell widely, with isolated totals over eight inches and rates meteorologists class as a once-in-200-years event. Roads were blocked by mudslides or washed out, propane tanks broke loose and floated downstream — one caught fire and exploded, lightly injuring a firefighter — and at least four structure fires broke out overnight.

Georgia's governor declared a state of emergency for four counties, Tennessee activated its operations center, and mandatory overnight curfews were imposed in flooded areas. Remarkably, officials reported no significant injuries or missing people by late Thursday — the rescue count, not a casualty count, is the story.

items.title: A judge blocks Trump's triumphal arch within an hour of its final approval
items.summary:
A federal judge blocked construction of President Trump's proposed triumphal arch late Thursday, less than an hour after the National Capital Planning Commission gave the 250-foot monument its final approval in an 8-4 vote. More than 120 citizens, many of them veterans, had testified across eight hours, most pleading with the panel to stop it.

U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan's temporary order, sought by the District of Columbia and Virginia, bars construction, excavation, demolition, utility work and road closures at the Memorial Circle site — the traffic island linking the Lincoln Memorial to Arlington National Cemetery — for 14 days while the court weighs the case.

The administration had said work could run 20 hours a day for two to three years and might begin immediately after the vote. In a 33-page opinion, the judge questioned the government's shifting justifications, including a late emphasis on national security, and found the local governments likely to be harmed — so the arch is approved on paper and frozen in fact, for now.

items.title: California's governor commutes every death sentence in the state — all 548 of them
items.summary:
Governor Gavin Newsom announced Thursday that he will commute the death sentences of all 548 people on California's death row to life in prison without parole — 529 men and 19 women. It is the largest mass commutation in American history, covering more than a quarter of the nation's condemned prisoners.

Newsom, who halted executions in 2019 shortly after taking office, said in an open letter that the death penalty is unjust and error-prone. The move does not repeal capital punishment — voters kept it in 2012 and 2016, and prosecutors can still seek it in new cases — and nobody is being released.

About 382 of the commutations, roughly 70 percent, still need California Supreme Court approval because those prisoners have more than one felony conviction. Newsom leaves office in January and is weighing a 2028 presidential run; his successor has said the execution moratorium will continue. No one has been executed in California since 2006.

items.title: East Coast faces heavy rain and flood risk Friday as a cross-country storm moves east
items.summary:
After weeks of dry weather, rain returns to the Northeast on Friday as the same cross-country storm system behind the Georgia–Tennessee flooding tracks up the coast. Forecasters expect rounds of showers and thunderstorms along the I-95 corridor, with more than an inch of rain in places and localized downpours that could trigger minor flooding.

The National Weather Service has flagged a slight risk of excessive rainfall from the Mid-Atlantic into southeastern New England, with a level-2 flash flood risk covering eastern Long Island, Providence and Boston. A flood watch is posted for Rhode Island and southeast Massachusetts, where one to three inches are expected and isolated spots could see four to five.

Friday morning's commute along I-95 is expected to be particularly wet, and parts of the Delmarva and the Carolinas could see severe afternoon storms with damaging gusts and an isolated tornado. Most of the East Coast dries out by Saturday afternoon — this is a one-day soaking, not a weekend washout.

items.title: Amy Acton defeats Vivek Ramaswamy — Ohio's first woman elected governor — and Sherrod Brown is heading back to the Senate
items.summary:
The certified picture from Tuesday is now clear: Democrat Amy Acton beat Republican Vivek Ramaswamy for governor, 2,404,178 votes to 2,039,730 with nearly 98 percent of precincts reporting. Acton is the first woman elected governor of Ohio and the first Democrat to win the office since 2006.

Sherrod Brown completed the sweep in the special Senate election, defeating Jon Husted 2,301,042 to 2,077,748. Brown, who spent 30 years in Congress before losing in 2024, flips a Republican seat and helped deliver the Democratic Senate majority. Democrats also flipped at least two Ohio U.S. House seats and the secretary of state's office.

Acton takes office January 11. Results stay unofficial until counties certify — Cuyahoga County's certification is scheduled for November 24 — but the margins leave no realistic path for the outcomes to change.

items.title: Cuyahoga County voters approve the health and human services levies, and re-elect Ronayne
items.summary:
Cuyahoga County voters backed both social-services levies on Tuesday by wide margins: Issue 10 for developmental disabilities passed with nearly 63 percent, and Issue 11 for health and human services with about 60 percent. County Executive Chris Ronayne, who championed both, also won an uncontested second term the same night.

The trade-off is explicit: roughly $166 to $170 more per year for every $100,000 of home value, in exchange for about $210 million in 2027 funding spread over the next decade for foster care, job-search help, developmental-disability services and mental health support. County leaders pitched the levies as backfilling federal cuts, though they do not cover the whole shortfall.

Voters also approved charter changes limiting some executive powers, and a Democratic win in County Council District 5 leaves the council with no Republican members. Locally, this was less a close call than a statement: the county chose to tax itself rather than shrink the safety net.

items.title: The feds deny Cleveland a $7.8 million lead-safe grant after rating the city too risky
items.summary:
The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development has turned down Cleveland's application for a $7.8 million lead hazard grant — money meant to make local homes lead-safe. Signal Cleveland reports the denial was not about need: HUD's risk review rated the city itself too risky to manage the funds, based on its performance across several federal housing grants, not just lead programs.

The timing is awkward. Three older HUD lead grants are winding down at once — a $9.7 million Glenville grant closing this month, a $2 million healthy-homes grant ending next June, and a $5.7 million citywide grant ending next July — and no replacement money is lined up behind them.

City officials are seeking a debriefing, checking whether an appeal is possible, and hunting for other funding. One thing does not change: property owners' Lead Safe Certificate obligations stay exactly as they are, grant or no grant.

items.title: Glenville's playoff run ends after an appeals court sides with the OHSAA
items.summary:
Glenville High School's football season is over. On Thursday, Ohio's Eighth District Court of Appeals granted the OHSAA an emergency stay, undoing a lower-court order that had put the Tarblooders back into the Division III playoffs and reinstating their October 29 removal while the appeal plays out.

The fight centers on Ginn Academy, a magnet school with no athletics of its own, and how the Cleveland school district documented where 10 of its student-athletes live and which school they play for. The trial judge had called the removal arbitrary because the OHSAA acted before finishing its investigation or declaring any player ineligible.

For the bracket, the consequence is immediate: Salem hosts University School tonight at 7 p.m. in the second round, with University advancing in Glenville's place. Glenville finishes 8-2 — a defending state champion from last year, eliminated by paperwork and a court calendar rather than on the field.

items.title: Democrat Brian Poindexter unseats Rep. Max Miller in Ohio's 7th District
items.summary:
One of Tuesday's biggest local upsets came in Ohio's 7th Congressional District, where Democrat Brian Poindexter defeated Republican Representative Max Miller, 54.1 percent to 45.9 percent. This is a district Donald Trump carried by 11 points in 2024, and Miller himself won it that year by 15.

Miller's campaign never escaped its own headlines, including domestic-violence allegations from his ex-wife and a public feud with his ex-father-in-law. Republican senators had called on him to resign, but he stayed in the race too long for the party to replace him — stepping aside would simply have left Poindexter unopposed.

The result fits the night's pattern across Northeast Ohio, but it stands out on its own: safe-seat incumbency protected Miller through the primary season and then collapsed in the general. District voters will get a freshman representative in January, and the seat becomes an instant 2028 target.

items.title: Strongsville, North Royalton and Olmsted Falls approve fire and EMS levies
items.summary:
Three Cuyahoga County suburbs voted Tuesday to pay for their own fire and ambulance services. Strongsville approved Issue 103, a new 1-mill continuing fire levy, with 56 percent support — the money is earmarked primarily to hire 12 additional firefighter-paramedics.

North Royalton's Issue 57 passed with about 56 percent: it renews the existing 1.7-mill EMS levy and adds 0.3 mill, creating a 2-mill levy for five years from tax year 2027 worth roughly $2.27 million a year. Olmsted Falls renewed its fire levy with 60 percent support, while rejecting a separate income-tax increase on the same ballot.

Read together with the county's big social-services levies, Tuesday's pattern in the suburbs was consistent: voters said yes to funding the services that show up at their door, even in a year when they were punishing incumbents almost everywhere else.

baby.tip: Day 5 tip — the paperwork one, while it's quiet: Benji needs to be added to the health plan, and newborn enrollment windows are usually short, so it's worth a call to the fund office to confirm the exact deadline and what they need (typically the birth certificate or hospital record). One short call now beats a scramble later — and ask his pediatrician's office what they need on file too.
baby.fact: At five days old, Benji already knows his favorite scent — newborns can recognize their mother's smell within days of birth and will turn toward it. His hearing is tuned the same way: the voices he's heard most, yours and Kelly's, are the ones that settle him fastest.
baby.fun: Name tidbit for Day 5: Benjamin means 'son of the right hand' in Hebrew — traditionally the favored spot. Tiny mission to match: one photo today of Benji in someone's right-arm cradle hold, Moose supervising from a polite distance.
